title: Water Infrastructure Security
scope_note: US drinking-water and wastewater cyber-physical security. This is a research map, not a live threat feed, compliance certification, or procurement ranking.
funding_note: No defensible national total exists. Published federal, state, and local spending mixes security with broader resilience and infrastructure. Amounts below keep selected awards, available programs, and purchases separate and never count a broad eligibility pool as security spending.

threats.title: Internet-exposed PLC compromise
threats.evidence: IRGC-affiliated CyberAv3ngers compromised Unitronics PLCs used by US water and wastewater systems, focusing on internet-exposed devices with default or absent passwords. Investigators observed operational manipulation, including deleted ladder logic.
threats.why_it_matters: One exposed controller can bridge an internet intrusion into pumps, valves, alarms, or chemical processes.

threats.title: Insider and former-contractor access
threats.evidence: A former instrumentation and control technician was federally charged after allegedly retaining remote access to Discovery Bay, California, uninstalling the main operational and monitoring system, and shutting down supporting servers.
threats.why_it_matters: Offboarding, named accounts, privilege limits, and monitored remote access are operational controls, not paperwork.

sources.label: US Attorney, Northern District of California

threats.title: Ransomware and IT-to-OT propagation
threats.evidence: GAO found that attacks have disrupted water operations and that legacy equipment, workforce gaps, and limited voluntary investment constrain defenses where business IT connects to operational technology.
threats.why_it_matters: Segmentation, tested recovery, and safe manual operation matter as much as detecting malware.

threats.title: Physical intrusion and intentional contamination
threats.evidence: Credible physical pathways include breached fences and hatches, access to finished water, sabotage of remote facilities, and theft or forced release of dangerous treatment chemicals.
threats.why_it_matters: Cameras alone do not close the loop; detection must connect to staffed response, water-quality monitoring, and practiced investigation procedures.

sources.label: CISA ChemLock water and wastewater fact sheet

capabilities.title: Baseline OT hygiene
capabilities.description: Remove unnecessary public exposure; inventory IT and OT; replace defaults; use strong authentication; patch or compensate; segment networks; maintain tested backups; and exercise response and recovery.
capabilities.limit: Passive monitoring tools do not replace architecture, identity, recovery, or operator practice.

capabilities.title: Utility assessment and mitigation planning
capabilities.description: EPA offers free drinking-water, wastewater, and combined-system cybersecurity evaluations covering IT and OT, followed by a gap report and risk-mitigation-plan template.
capabilities.limit: Assessment and planning are not implementation funding or continuous defense. EPA says it receives anonymized aggregate results, not utility-specific findings.

sources.label: EPA Water Sector Cybersecurity Evaluation Program

capabilities.title: Secure OT remote access
capabilities.description: NIST SP 1800-45 gives utilities a replicable reference architecture for remote access to water and wastewater operational technology.
capabilities.limit: A reference implementation is not proof that utilities or participating vendors have deployed every control.

capabilities.title: Physical monitoring and contamination response
capabilities.description: Layer facility hardening, door and hatch sensors, alarms, cameras, secure communications, water-quality sensors, complaint surveillance, public-health notification, and practiced investigation procedures.
capabilities.limit: Sensors must be commissioned, maintained, and tied to humans with authority to respond.

capabilities.title: Threat sharing and mutual aid
capabilities.description: WaterISAC distributes sector intelligence; state WARN networks move personnel, equipment, materials, and services between utilities during emergencies.
capabilities.limit: These networks do not amount to a uniform national security operations center or mandatory telemetry from every utility.

companies.name: Dragos
companies.category: OT asset discovery, monitoring, threat detection, incident response, training
companies.evidence: Placer County Water Agency authorized a sole-source Dragos OT platform purchase up to $87,590 in August 2025 for asset discovery, network visibility, and threat correlation; Dragos was already under contract for incident response.
companies.evidence_limit: Named public procurement proves one deployment, not national market share or comparative superiority.

sources.label: Placer County Water Agency board item

companies.name: Claroty
companies.category: Cyber-physical asset inventory, exposure management, secure access, monitoring
companies.evidence: Claroty reports a deployment at an unnamed US water supplier serving more than two million people, covering asset, session, process, and risk visibility.
companies.evidence_limit: Customer identity and outcomes are vendor-reported and not independently verifiable from the cited case study.

companies.name: Nozomi Networks
companies.category: OT/IoT inventory, anomaly detection, risk scoring, vulnerability prioritization
companies.evidence: Nozomi publishes a water-specific platform and an anonymous large-US-utility deployment.
companies.evidence_limit: No fetched public procurement or named US water deployment established adoption scale; treat it as a candidate supplier, not proven nationwide coverage.

companies.name: Waterfall Security Solutions
companies.category: Unidirectional gateways and physically enforced IT-OT data flow
companies.evidence: Waterfall offers one-way gateways for water-treatment SCADA, remote monitoring, and external data access, physically constraining inbound connectivity rather than only detecting it.
companies.evidence_limit: Fetched evidence is vendor-authored; no named US municipal deployment, price, or measured outcome was verified.

public_players.name: EPA Office of Water and Office of Research and Development
public_players.role: Water-sector risk-management lead: assessments, technical assistance, AWIA resilience requirements, contamination-response tools, physical-security guidance, financing alignment, and research.
public_players.boundary: Wastewater systems and drinking-water systems serving 3,300 or fewer people generally lack equivalent mandatory cyber risk-assessment requirements.

public_players.name: CISA and FBI
public_players.role: Cross-sector threat intelligence, advisories, external vulnerability scanning, incident support, investigation, and law-enforcement response.
public_players.boundary: They are not water regulators and do not continuously defend every utility.

public_players.name: NIST National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence
public_players.role: Turns standards into reproducible laboratory architectures; its 2026 water guide focuses on secure OT remote access.
public_players.boundary: NIST validates architectures; it does not certify products or fund deployment.

sources.label: NIST water and wastewater operations project

public_players.name: EPA Water Security Test Bed at Idaho National Laboratory
public_players.role: Full-scale, reconfigurable drinking-water distribution test bed for controlled contamination, decontamination, disaster-response, and emerging cyber-physical experiments.
public_players.boundary: The existing public record emphasizes contamination and recovery; a broader OT product-testing mission is proposed, not current coverage.

public_players.name: DOE CyTRICS national-laboratory network
public_players.role: Standardized testing of priority OT product software and firmware, component enumeration, shared findings, vendor agreements, and managed vulnerability disclosure.
public_players.boundary: CyTRICS currently serves the energy sector. It is a transferable model, not an existing water program, and it is not an LLNL-only facility.

sources.label: DOE Cyber Testing for Resilient Industrial Control Systems

public_players.name: WaterISAC and state WARN networks
public_players.role: Trusted intelligence exchange plus established utility-to-utility mutual aid for personnel, equipment, materials, and services.
public_players.boundary: Participation and capacity vary; neither network replaces agency authority or product testing.

public_players.name: State primacy agencies, CIOs, homeland-security offices, and SRF administrators
public_players.role: Translate national capability into utility cohorts, financing, operator training, exercises, incident coordination, and local implementation.
public_players.boundary: Capacity is uneven; a national program must fund delivery rather than assume every state has water-OT specialists.

sources.label: Water Sector Cybersecurity Task Force recommendations

investments.program: EPA Midsize and Large Drinking Water System Infrastructure Resilience and Sustainability
investments.scope: Ten resilience projects. At least $2,564,875 is clearly cyber-focused: Lake City, Florida SCADA/pump controls ($189,875) and San Diego PLC replacement ($2.375 million). Other mixed projects may include cyber work, but their security share is not separable.
investments.anti_double_count_note: The $2.564875 million subset sits inside, not on top of, the $11.75 million total.

investments.program: New York SECURE water and wastewater cybersecurity grants
investments.scope: Assessment grants up to $50,000 with no match and implementation awards up to $100,000, paired with tiered state cyber standards and technical assistance.
investments.anti_double_count_note: Available program funding; the amount awarded by 2026-09-21 was not verified.

investments.program: Placer County Water Agency Dragos procurement
investments.scope: Agency-wide operations funding for a named OT-security platform.
investments.anti_double_count_note: Do not add to federal or state grant totals unless reimbursement is later documented.

sources.label: Placer County Water Agency board item

investments.scope: Texas, the White House Office of the National Cyber Director, EPA, CISA, and private partners launched a pilot providing assessments, remediation, and defensive tools to participating utilities at no cost.
investments.anti_double_count_note: Useful operating-model evidence, not quantified investment evidence; the official page gives no public budget, utility count, vendor roster, or measured result.

precedents.name: EPA/INL Water Security Test Bed
precedents.lesson: Start with a real cyber-physical proving ground where destructive testing is safe; add representative PLCs, pumps, telemetry, remote access, vendor firmware, and physical intrusion scenarios.

precedents.name: DOE CyTRICS
precedents.lesson: Reuse standardized intake, test protocols, vendor agreements, findings formats, component taxonomy, protected analytics, and managed disclosure for a Water-CyTRICS track.

precedents.name: LLNL Skyfall and CyTRICS analytics
precedents.lesson: Pair INL's water loop with hardware-in-the-loop simulation and cross-product software, firmware, and bill-of-materials analysis; never connect research systems to utility production.

precedents.name: ORNL Grid Operations and Analytics Laboratory
precedents.lesson: Use governed operational feeds or replayable derived datasets from willing utilities instead of relying only on synthetic networks.

precedents.name: EPA evaluation and technical-assistance programs
precedents.lesson: Use EPA as the front door; preserve utility control of detailed findings and use de-identified aggregates for national prioritization.

precedents.name: Anthropic Project Glasswing
precedents.lesson: Begin with a screened cohort, require remediation capacity before testing, coordinate disclosure, measure fixed vulnerabilities rather than findings alone, then expand.

precedents.name: OpenAI Daybreak
precedents.lesson: Separate routine defensive support from higher-risk validation, deliver through trusted partners and workflows, and subsidize access for public and small critical-infrastructure operators.

precedents.name: Texas Project Watershed 250
precedents.lesson: A state can convene federal and private capabilities into a no-cost utility pilot, but publish participation, spending, remediation, and outcome measures if the model is to be evaluated.

proposal.name: Project Confluence
proposal.tagline: Where water operations, national laboratories, states, and defenders meet.
proposal.mission: Reduce the likelihood and public-health consequences of cyber, physical, supply-chain, and compound attacks on drinking-water and wastewater systems by joining EPA's utility relationships and financing channels with DOE laboratory testing, CISA threat and incident capabilities, state delivery networks, vendor remediation, and utility operations.
proposal.leadership: EPA is accountable lead because water is its sector responsibility. DOE co-leads laboratory testing and cyber-physical research. CISA owns cross-sector threat support and incident coordination, not water regulation.
proposal.governance: Begin with a five-year EPA-DOE interagency agreement and a CISA operating annex. Use the existing Water Government Coordinating Council and Water Sector Coordinating Council for oversight, with a technical steering committee representing states, tribes, utilities of every size and ownership model, WaterISAC, WARNs, public health, labs, vendors, integrators, and independent researchers.

service_lines.name: Assess
service_lines.description: EPA cyber and physical evaluation, asset inventory, external exposure review, dependency mapping, and recovery baseline.

service_lines.name: Test
service_lines.description: Water-CyTRICS component testing, firmware and software composition analysis, hardware-in-the-loop simulation, contamination trials, and patch validation.

service_lines.name: Exercise
service_lines.description: Operator and executive exercises combining cyber intrusion, physical access, contamination, power and communications loss, manual operation, and WARN mobilization.

service_lines.name: Fix
service_lines.description: Prioritized implementation, vendor remediation sprints, segmentation, secure remote access, backup restoration, procurement clauses, and financing support.

service_lines.name: Share
service_lines.description: Protected WaterISAC advisories, component exposure notices, de-identified trends, state briefings, and public post-remediation lessons.

proposal.regional_model: Launch four nodes, then scale toward one delivery partnership in every EPA region. Each pairs a state lead, national-lab team, utility or university training site, WaterISAC, and WARN. Nodes bring mobile assessment and test kits, exercises, operator training, vendor remediation clinics, and small-system implementation support.

roles.role: Utility intake, eligibility, assessments, water-quality scenarios, state coordination, technical assistance, financing alignment, and translation of findings into operator guidance.
Common test protocols; product, firmware, and supply-chain analysis; cyber-physical experiments; digital twins; safe validation; research-to-deployment transition.
Threat intelligence, vulnerability coordination, scanning, incident escalation, investigation, and cross-sector dependency support.

roles.actor: States, tribes, WaterISAC, WARNs, and utilities
roles.role: Set priorities, select representative cohorts, validate operational practicality, train operators, finance upgrades, share lessons, and provide mutual aid.
Provide products, firmware, bills of materials, documentation, engineering support, mitigations, customer notices, secure configurations, and end-of-support dates under standard agreements.

milestones.targets: Agreement and disclosure rules; four regional nodes; five states and 50 utilities; 25 high-prevalence product families inventoried; 15 tested; 10 combined exercises; first anonymized baseline.
Delivery presence in every EPA region; 500 utilities served; 100 product families tested; 75% of confirmed high-severity findings mitigated within agreed windows; 2,500 people trained.

2,000 utilities served; protected national component-exposure map; shorter remediation and restoration times; mature protocols moved into procurement, curricula, vendor practice, and repeatable state programs; independent evaluation before permanent funding.

measures: Days from validated finding to vendor mitigation
Days from advisory to utility mitigation or compensating control
Removal of internet-exposed administration and default credentials
Tested backup restoration and safe manual-operation capability
Exercise time to detect, isolate, communicate, and restore
Repeat component exposures found across utilities
Small, rural, tribal, and disadvantaged-system participation
guardrails: Never connect offensive research systems to live water operations.
Use coordinated disclosure and emergency exceptions; measure remediation, not raw vulnerability counts.
Do not treat voluntary assessments as certifications or publicly rank utilities by vulnerability.
Minimize collected data; keep raw captures, credentials, and detailed diagrams with the utility unless it opts in.
No participant data for unrelated enforcement, commercial model training, or vendor marketing without separate authority.
Require human authorization for AI-assisted exploit validation and every operational change.
Give small, rural, tribal, and disadvantaged systems governance seats, not only services.
Vendor contributions cannot control test selection, findings, disclosure, or procurement.
funding_paths: Dedicated EPA-DOE appropriation for laboratories, regional delivery, mobile equipment, small-system support, and independent evaluation.
DWSRF/CWSRF and set-asides for eligible assessments, technical assistance, equipment, workforce, and resilience upgrades; these are eligibility paths, not security-only totals.
CISA state/local cyber grants where ownership and eligibility rules permit.
DOE CESER and laboratory research funding for reusable testing, analytics, and technology transition.
State/local appropriations, rates, bonds, and capital plans for sustained field implementation.
Vendor or philanthropic equipment and engineering support with strict conflict controls.
